# hpgsea

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pnnl/hpgsea/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pnnl/hpgsea/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Overview

The **hpgsea** R package provides a high-performance variant of gene-permutation gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) [@subramanian-gene-2005] that serves as a replacement for the Broad Institute's [ssGSEA2.0](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA2.0) repository (R package version by Nicole Gay: https://github.com/nicolerg/ssGSEA2).

Benchmarks showed that **hpgsea** was at least 15.21-fold faster than ssGSEA2.0. Furthermore, its speed, statistical power, and false positive rates were comparable to those of the popular [**fgsea**](https://bioconductor.org/packages//release/bioc/html/fgsea.html) R package [@korotkevich-fast-2021] across thousands of simulated datasets and 605 mouse and human datasets. Although **hpgsea** can not compute arbitrarily small P-values like **fgsea**, it has the advantage of being able to test bidirectional databases---those where each biomolecule in a set has an expected direction of change from prior experiments---like the Post-Translational Modification Signatures Database (PTMsigDB). (Note that the combination of **hpgsea** with PTMsigDB is known as PTM Signature Enrichment Analysis, or PTM-SEA [@krug-curated-2019].)

Moreover, while ssGSEA2.0's false positive rate is inflated because it unintentionally permutes the values of the genes, rather than their labels (see [this issue](https://github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA2.0/issues/45) for details), this is not the case with **hpgsea**.

All code to reproduce the results are provided in the manuscript/ directory. The data and results will be available for download from Zenodo in the near future.


## Installation

**macOS:** macOS users must install the [Xcode developer tools](https://mac.r-project.org/tools/) from Apple to compile C and C++ code.

**Windows:** Windows users must install [Rtools](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/) to compile C and C++ code.

**Linux:** No extra work should be necessary to install **hpgsea** on Linux, as most distributions already include a C/C++ compiler.

The development version of **hpgsea**, which requires R >= 4.0.0, can then be installed with

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("pnnl/hpgsea")
```

## Usage

### Simulate Data

We will simulate a vector of 10,000 signed gene-level statistics and a list of 20,000 gene sets by randomly sampling between 5 and 500 genes.

```{r simulate-data}
n_genes <- 1e4L # number of genes
genes <- paste0("gene", seq_len(n_genes))

# Simulate named vector of gene-level values
set.seed(9001L)
stats <- rnorm(n = n_genes)
names(stats) <- genes

# Simulate named list of gene sets
n_sets <- 2e4L
min_size <- 5L
max_size <- 500L
set_sizes <- rep(max_size:min_size, length.out = n_sets)

gene_sets <- lapply(seq_len(n_sets), function(i) {
  set.seed(i)
  sample(x = genes, size = set_sizes[i])
})
names(gene_sets) <- paste0("set", seq_along(gene_sets))
```

### Runtime and Results

This shows the runtime of `hpgsea` on an AMD Ryzen 5 7600X (Zen 4) CPU with its clock speed fixed at 4.7 GHz. A total of 1 million permutations were used to calculate P-values and normalized enrichment scores (NES).

```{r time-results}
library(hpgsea)

# Runtime (in seconds)
set.seed(0L)
system.time({
  res <- hpgsea(
    stats = stats,
    gene_sets = gene_sets,
    alpha = 1,
    nperm = 1e6L,
    min_size = min_size,
    max_size = max_size
  )
})

str(res)
```
